utterances.text: I think even everyone can give a proper answer to that, so let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, I have just one last area to ask you about. On the very first occasion that you were contacted about preparing this report, who were you contacted by, specifically? Was it the Defence, or was it somebody else?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the Defence. I was contacted by my superior in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were you specifically designated or requested by the Defence to prepare this report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if he was contacted by somebody other than the Defence, then it's without -- he wouldn't know whether or not he was specifically requested to do this work unless he was requested by the person that was contacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I can rephrase, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Defence asked specifically for you as opposed to anybody else to conduct this report?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Defence contacted the Ministry of the Interior, and my superior officer in the ministry chose me to carry out the assignment with the specifications given.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And prior to preparing this report, had you ever worked or had any contact with anyone on the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anybody from the Defence team before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. So, Mr. Markovic, we're finished with your testimony. It took longer than we expected, but it's all for a good cause. Before you leave this courtroom, I wish to thank you on behalf of my colleagues for having come over to the give testimony in this case, and we also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, documents or exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have four documents. 4D607, 617, 618, and 635.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. Just one addition to that. There is also the marked version of Annex A, which apparently has -- Annex 1, which apparently has been assigned a number by the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it there are no objections from any of the other Defence teams, so these documents are admitted. Anybody else wishes to tender documents? Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I've distributed the list. We have three documents, 3D513, 3DIC 233, and 3DIC 232. They were documents which the witness was shown in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic. Any objections, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objections from the Borovcanin team or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So these three documents are so admitted. Then we come to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think we've sent around a list of the documents to tender. There are several of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections, Mr. Gosnell? You are in possession of the list, I suppose. It's a 2-page list. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have objections as regard the document 3893.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The last one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely, my objection is related just to the second page of this document; namely, neither document from the second page is denoted on the first page of the document. So I don't believe that the second page of this document is the -- really the document -- it is really entire document. But the second page is just added to the first page of the document. I would -- I could explain it, Your Honours. Namely, there is working plan, for example; and it is on the second page. But on the first page, it was denoted that there is a copy -- a number 15, and on the second page there is copy number 1, and the second document was not denoted on the first page at all. It is a table of identifications or something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But rather than a question of admissibility, isn't that a submission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I can see the original of 3893.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Kwon. I can hand that up to the Court. All right, Your Honours. I'm sorry. I just want to -- I just want to tell you what I've given you, if I may. What I've given you is the copy of the first page, which is the letter from the -- to the command of the special police brigade that is signed for as received by Nedo Jovicic. You have the original of that. As well, you have a copy of the work plan Krivaja 95. You have a document that is indicated copy number 1, and you have also two copies of a document indicated copy number 1, and then you have another copy, number 12. My friend's objection is that the letter doesn't indicate that it's copy number 1 or 12. It indicates it's copy number 15. I'll address further matters as soon as you've had an opportunity to look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have several copies of copy number 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge Kwon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We have two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- two originals of copy 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, three originals. One is copy number 1, the second copy number 1, and a third copy number 12. That's correct. And they are all identical documents designated as the work plan related to Krivaja 95 as is indicated in the receipt signed by Nedo Jovicic. They are derived from the Drina Corps collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And do you have any comments, Mr. Vanderpuye, on the issue of the reference to number 15?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do. I just wanted to give you an opportunity to look at the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: I would benefit from your comments at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic. But let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's let Mr. Zivanovic finish what he has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to add that all these documents are from Drina Corps collection from the EDS, and they are confiscated when Drina Corps archive. But what is my point, I do not believe that these three specific pages are attached -- generally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- attached to the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to repeat the point because we got it when you first said it. I will soon give you the floor, Mr. Gosnell, but in the meantime let's hear what Mr. Vanderpuye has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Possibly, you could also address the aspect of whether these were recovered together, attached as one document or whether they have been made up to exist together.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the latter point first, I can't tell you specifically in what order they were actually seised. That, I don't know, and I can find that out for you at this moment. But they are designated and they are numbered in sequence as they are stamped, as they are date-stamped, the ERN numbers. I will also point out that there are two aspects that I think merit attention. Once is that the letter -- sorry, the receipt that is signed for by Nedo Jovicic designates the copies that he received of the relevant plans; that is, throughout the code book, the work plan, identification signals, and so on. What I want to bring to the Court's attention is that that document is a receipt, which necessarily implies that the document that is described in it went with the receiver, and that's the reason why it is not located in the Drina Corps collection. I would also point out that the receipt itself designates the work plan by name, Krivaja 95, and in that Drina Corps collection you find a work plan, Krivaja 95, and you can see multiple copies of it. We certainly suggest that there multiple copies, one of which went to the recipient that signed for it in the receipt. The other basis of admissibility with respect to this document, even separately, independently from the receipt, is that it is a document that sets forth a plan of communication that is directly relevant to the events that occurred in this case, directly relevant to the Defence in this case as concerns Mr. Borovcanin's ability to communicate with his subordinate units and other units in the area, and is directly relevant to this witness's testimony as a communications officer who is certainly capable of recognizing, deciphering, and interpreting this document as a separate issue. So for all of these bases, we would submit that it is admissible, and I think it is sufficiently identified in the record, also, to establish its -- its relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You should also bear in mind that Mr. Borovcanin has stated that, in fact, he reported to the Drina Corps on 11 July, and that's at the forward command post in Pribicevac. He also has stated that he went there to receive orders. This is dated the same day, and it is from the same corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I could see while you were addressing the Chamber that Mr. McCloskey wished to tell you something.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have been informed that I heard him, so I think we've covered everything. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My friend made a lot of remarks that I obviously strongly disagree with, characterizations. I won't take an issue with them now. In fact, I'm happy to tell you that we have no objection to P3893 coming into evidence. I would, however, like to reserve my position in respect of the other documents so I can have a chance to review them and ensure whether they're -- that they're admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We are pretty much fine-tuned here. It was really whether they are admitted as one document or whether they are admitted separately as two documents, is beside the point. To us, what is important is that we have heard the submission because ultimately it's a question of weight that we would attach to the witness's testimony, the Prosecution's position, and the documents that we have seen, and also the submission made by Mr. Zivanovic. So we'll weigh everything at the end of the day. So they will be admitted separately at this point in time to make things easier. The rest we will hear from you when, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If I could have the Chamber's indulgence until tomorrow morning, I would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are going to have a long break, as well, between now and this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me of that, Mr. President; and in light of that, yes, I'll get back to you at the beginning of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can use one of these small rooms at the back of Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where you will have fresh air and all the rest. This goes back to the Prosecution. Thank you. Perhaps any one of the Defence teams wishes to have a look at these three documents or not? Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. One moment, I know what you are saying, but my colleagues are not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's try once again. I just wanted to know whether we can continue now. I have a -- I have procedural material at hand. Last Friday, we received some documents containing intercepts. I'm not asking for the hearing to be interrupted; rather, I wanted to say something different. This concerns intercepts from 1992 and up to 1994. Those intercepts were in the possession of the Prosecutor's Office since 2003. What I am worried about is the following: Why are we only receiving those documents now this late in the proceedings? They do not relate directly to the period of the indictment. These documents have been in the possession of the Prosecution for six years or so. I did see some of those documents when we had witnesses discussing them, and it was rather difficult to locate them in the EDS. Our resources are not limitless, and we cannot spend much time analysing those thousands upon thousands of pages. I don't know what the aim of the Prosecution is concerning those intercepts. That's why I would like to ask the Chamber to issue an order to the Prosecution to see whether this has anything to do with rule 68 or whether this can be dealt with during cross-examination. Perhaps these documents will be used by the Prosecution after the Defence has replied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I don't know what documents you are referring to. Mr. McCloskey perhaps can enlighten us on this and also explain your position trying to answer Ms. Fauveau's query.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. These are documents from periods not directly related to indictment that she said, 92 through 94. We just identified them in a -- and they were given to us in a hard copy format, and they were not filed in the intercept section. So we stumbled across them within the last week or two and decided to put them on the EDS so they could be looked at for whatever value they might have by anyone if any, given the time-frame that they're from, and I would think counsel would want us to alert them to potentially relevant documents. I don't see anything overtly incriminating or exculpatory about that time-period, but there was one interesting intercept we had seen, and we alerted the counsel -- one counsel to that, and if we find any more, we will alert them to them. And we have hard copies available in some 12 binders if they want to come look at them, if they want to do a little historical research into those years. But I think it's a storm in a teacup. It's unfortunate that we find material like this late, but it happens, and it's not in 1995. So I don't really see that it's a major issue. If we find something, we'll let people know about it, but I think it's important they have it to look themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't want to create a problem concerning these intercepts. In ten days, I have to begin with my case. I have now received over 11.000 pages. When one is faced with such a disclosure, you can guess that there are relevant materials among those. Of course, I believe the Prosecutor does not disclose all of the material they have; otherwise, it would be impossible to go through. I just want to know whether there is any material from the collection that they intend to use and with what aim, and perhaps they can indicate what the year is or the collection is. They should find a way to indicate to us what they are going to look into since we cannot study 11.000 pages. I agree with my learned friend that these documents are -- do not relate to the period of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We fully understand, of course, the problem raised by Madam Fauveau as well as the explanation given by Mr. McCloskey for the Prosecution. At the moment, I think there is very little, if anything at all, that we can do. I suppose we will intervene if asked at a later stage. If, indeed, this becomes a problem to you, Madam Fauveau, if you realise that you need to add witnesses, whatever. I mean, we have been very receptive in the past on similar issues, and we won't change when it comes to your case. So let's leave it for the time being. In the meantime, if there is someone from the Prosecution that has got a bird's eye view of the contents of these documents and can at least give an indication of what they are about, that, of course, would help. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just -- they are much like the 95 documents. They cover a huge range of materials, most of which don't have any relevancy. Like even the '95 documents don't really have much -- most of them don't have much relevancy to these events. So that's the same true of '92, '93, and '94. We are going through a process of indexing them, so we will get a better picture of who's speaking to who and who's mentioned. And as we get that material, as we always do, we get it over to the Defence so they can help make some sense out of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's fair enough, and we'll come to it later on if it's the case. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, now I'm in the possession of the original version of P3893. We still have no objection to it being admitted, but there are some strange physical characteristics of this document, such as there seem to be two different pages that have been cut from another document and then taped; and then subsequent to that, there was photocopying. Now, I know nothing about how any of this happened. I merely want to make sure that anything that is admitted, that somehow there is a record of what the physical condition of this apparent original is, unless there's some explanation from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Having heard you say that, perhaps it will be better if the Prosecution in tendering this document, apart from the two pages that we saw before, will have the full -- the entire four pages, that is, the handwritten page plus the two versions number 1 and number 12, have them photocopied and -- yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We will do that. We're always open to go down to the vault and pick out the original materials as they were collected and stamped if any of these little mysteries can be resolved, though I think someone does have Milenko Jevdjevic, the Drina Corps comms person, on their witness list who was at Pribicevac at the time, so perhaps some of the mysteries will be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So you'll come back to us on the rest in the afternoon? Good. Any other objections from any of the other Defence teams? None. So that chapter is closed. We were reminded a minute ago that there is still an outstanding list that the Borovcanin Defence team intends to tender in relation to the previous witness 4DPW002 -- oh, sorry, 4DW020, or 4DPW002. You know who the guy is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have distributed a tender list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I need to say more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objections, Mr. Vanderpuye? If you also want to take your time and respond in the afternoon session when we start, that's okay with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a good idea. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes. We have a communication from the chief of security in relation to what you raised earlier on. The idea of having doors left open and free circulation possible is not acceptable; and as I was telling Judge Prost, having thought in my career not to argue with the Defence because they may have reasons of their own -- with security because they have their own reasons, so I am not prepared -- my colleagues are not prepared to argue with them. The other one is there is a slight mistake here. It seems to me that they do agree for Mr. Borovcanin to swap cell with Mr. Gvero. Here it's written the other way around, Mr. Gvero to go in the smaller cell and Mr. Borovcanin to go to the larger cell. But of course, it's a misunderstanding, and so that's how it will be. There will be the arrangements later on. I am sure the security officers who will be on duty with the accused at the time when we go to the break will have instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, although why in principle Mr. Borovcanin should have to spend his time in that room rather than my client, I don't know, but I don't represent him; and he's very kindly made that offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Our next witness is Professor Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Professor Dunjic. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know the procedure, so let's proceed with the solemn declaration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Professor. Please take your seat. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Welcome back, Professor Dunjic. Now, sir, you've previously testified before this Chamber, so I'd like to start by simply asking you to give a bird's eye view or an overview of the subject matter of the report that you have now prepared and given to the Court.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The subject matter of the research for which I am present here was to analyse the locations in Potocari; to also analyse the autopsy reports of the exhumations, including the Sandici location.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Just so that we understand what it is precisely that you reviewed --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- can we please look at -- can we please have 4D540 on the screen, please. It's 4D540, and if we could have page 57 of the English and page 31 in e-court of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, making reference to this part of your report, can you explain to the Chamber the autopsy and exhumation records that you reviewed in respect of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I reviewed the material that has to do with the Potocari location. I found out that the exhumations were done in 2006 when most of the bodies were exhumed as well as in 2005 when three corpses were exhumed and assigned their respective numbers and in 2004 when one person was exhumed with its own identification number. One concludes from that that at the location there were several, and we can see here that there were three, exhumations. I had occasion to review the autopsy reports, which have to do with the location at which bodies were exhumed in 2006 when seven bodies were extracted as well as additional bones. I will explain that in detail later. I also studied the autopsy reports pertaining to the location from 2004, and that includes that single case I mentioned; and I subsequently received the autopsy report, which I reviewed. That is as far as the number of cases goes that I could locate in the reports as well as the number of exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So it in grand total --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So in grand total, how many cases did you review in respect of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: There was a total of 11 cases across the three locations, 7 cases from 2006, 3 from 2005, and 1 from 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, I want to ask you about two specific categories of findings that were contained in the autopsy reports that you reviewed - and we'll get into this in more detail - but at first, I would like you to just focus on these two specific sets of findings. In respect of the cause of death and the evidence of injury, can you tell the Court what the findings were in those autopsy reports of bodies exhumed from these graves at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The autopsies and exhumations concerning Potocari dating from 2006 concerning these cases have one basic characteristic, and that is the cause of death that is missing with all of the cases. As for any evidence of injury, as stated in the autopsy reports, it is insufficient. There is no proof that can be viewed as relevant in order to establish the type of injury. That is the basic characteristic of these exhumed cases from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right, sir. Before we continue, let me just return to your first answer about the number of bodies at Potocari because when I look at your report, I notice that there is a series of numbers there that appear to refer to cases, and it says "POT 01 SRE 001 to POT 01 SRE 10." So were there ten cases, or were there seven cases, or could you perhaps clarify my confusion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The numbers you see concern all of the bones and bodies found at the location ranging from 1 to 10; however, these were not ten individuals. As a matter of fact, there were six males that can be identified through the use of autopsy reports, and there is an additional skull that belonged to a female. There were seven persons in total at that location. The designation Potocari 7 and 8, those two numbers were actually used for two sets of bones, which were later matched to form a single person through various means of identification. That is why we are talking about seven bodies. Number 9 and number 10 are parts of bones of an arm. In one case, these are bones from two arms; and in the other case, we have bones of a single arm. There is no DNA identification report of those bones. Therefore, we don't know whether these bones, marked with 9 and 10, belong to any of the persons previously marked with the numbers 1 through to 9 or these were completely separate bones of different people. In any case, we have six male and one female corpse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Now, the translation that I received of your answer when I asked you about the findings in respect of these two categories, cause of death and evidence of injury, it came through to me that you said that it was not present. Now, were findings actually reached in these reports which indicated something about these two categories, or were they just left blank?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, evidence of injury -- well, there is a chapter in the autopsy report template. When one looks at it, you realise that there is a form with its individual chapters. There is a chapter reading proof of injury or evidence of injury. In that chapter, there should be findings. As regards the Srebrenica cases, there is only one case under number 7, which mentions any evidence of injury. In all the other six cases, it is stated that there is no evidence of injury. This was written that there is no evidence under that chapter, evidence of injury. It says "none" or "not established." It is for that reason that I said that as regards the cause of death, for that particular case it is correctly stated that there was no cause of death, or rather, to put it in other words, that the cause of death could not be ascertained. Perhaps I can translate into your legal language. The finding as stated in the autopsy report corresponds to -- corresponds with the conclusion arrived at. There is a consistency between the conclusion stating that the cause of death was not ascertained because, in the report, no injuries are entered. This corresponds between the two documents, and that is something that is characteristic for the Potocari location.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was cause of death ascertained in any of the ten autopsy reports that you reviewed in respect of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: No. It was not ascertained.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Let's go directly now to the cases that you reviewed at Sandici meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could scroll to page 62 in e-court in the B/C/S version and page 116 in the English vision, and I hope that's correct, but there is a real problem with the pagination of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell us how many cases you reviewed of grave sites at Sandici? I'm sorry. Perhaps I can assist you. It will be page 61 in your -- in the copy of your report.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I have to admit that the Sandici location posed some problems in that I had reports and various documents that I referred to. These stated that there were exhumations in the area of Sandici in 2000, 2001, 2002, 2005, and 2004. In 2004, at the location there were 17 bodies that were exhumed; in 2000, there were three; in 2001, there was one case; in 2002, there was one case; and in 2005, another single case, a total of 23. These were basically five different locations, and I had the autopsy reports pertaining to the location concerning 2004 mentioning 17 cases. I did note my remarks concerning the marking of bodies, which can cause a lot of confusion subsequently in the process of identification and comparing the findings, since these cases were simply marked in different ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We have to stop here. Professor Dunjic, we will continue at 3.00 or thereabouts in the afternoon. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. For the record, now the Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Mitchell; and in addition to the absentees from the Defence teams, there is now Mr. Bourgon absent too. Yes. Let's continue. Mr. Gosnell -- sorry, Mr. McCloskey. I didn't see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. So we don't forget, we don't have any -- any objections to the exhibits of Stojcinovic Defence witness. We've had a chance to look at those now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Just a footnote to that, there are two exhibits on the tender list that apparently have already been admitted. Those are 4D253 and 4D260.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And I need to -- Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Any objections from anyone in relation to this list? None. So all these documents are admitted, and 260 and 253 are not to be included in the list because they have already been admitted. And you also had to give us feedback, Mr. Gosnell, on the Prosecution's list of exhibits in relation to your previous witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we will be objecting to four of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But let's proceed with the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then we will take that up later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor Dunjic. Now, we left off -- just before we left off, you indicated that you had reviewed autopsy reports related to Sandici in respect of 17 sets of remains; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that's what is described at page 61 -- or summarised, I should say, at page 61 in the B/C/S version of your report and on page 50 of the English version of your report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Now, I would like to ask you the same question about these 17 autopsy reports that I asked you in relation to the ten autopsy reports that you reviewed in respect of Potocari. In particular, can you please describe for us the findings that were reached in respect of cause of death and in respect of evidence of injury?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. As opposed to the Potocari location, the one at Sandici concerning the 17 cases that I analysed is characteristic of the fact that in all those 17 cases there was a conclusion on the cause of death, and that in all of the 17 cases, there was evidence of injury. However, I should add the following: The conclusion about the cause of death at the Sandici location is inconsistent with the finding from the autopsy reports because we have injuries described there on the bones, which are inconsistent with gunshot wounds, and the conclusion is formulated for all the 17 cases stating that with a certain degree of probability these people were injured by firearms, hence the inconsistency. As for evidence of injury, in that particular chapter of the autopsy report - and I will remind you again that the form used was identical to the one in Potocari - in any case, in that chapter, evidence of injury, the injuries were described in the same identical fashion as they were in the Potocari case, but now it is put in a separate chapter as "proof of injury," in quotation marks. Concerning these -- this "proof of injury," out of all the cases, there are only three with registered changes to the bones, which indicate that there had been gunshot injuries. For example, there are five or six injuries described in five or six different parts of bodies in the 17 cases. There are only three bones out of the total number -- there are only three cases of three bones exhibiting evidence that can be related to gunshot injuries. That amounts to the inconsistency between the finding and the conclusion on the cause of death. That would be put in the briefest possible terms concerning Sandici.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So I understand you to be saying, then, that with the exception of those three cases at Sandici that you just mentioned, the remaining 14 cases, in terms of the nature of the descriptions in the autopsy reports, is the nature of those descriptions different or the same or similar to what you observed when you read the autopsy reports from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I must say that the description of injuries at Sandici, since the same team worked on both Potocari and Sandici, their description of injuries at Sandici, they say that this is proof of injury or evidence of injury; and they used the identical terms they did with certain findings from Potocari. However, as for the Potocari cases, there were no conclusions on the cause of death because it was unascertainable as stated by the expert. However, in the Sandici cases they decidedly stated that there were gunshot wounds amounting to the cause of death. These were two different things that we need to establish, the manner of injuries and the cause of death; and I believe that in the state the bones were, it was impossible to ascertain, even in the three cases where there were changes to the bones allegedly caused by gunshot injuries. The degree of damage to the bones is of such a high level that in my view it is not possible to prove that these resulted from gunshot injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say in your report that the inability to find cause of death or the indication that cause of death was indetermined -- or indeterminate at Potocari, you say in your report that such a formulate cause of death is acceptable. Would you say that the formulate cause of death indicated in the Sandici autopsy reports was acceptable?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. From the forensic point of view, the professional point of view, the doctrine point of view of forensic pathology, the conclusions, as they are with the Sandici location, for all the 17 cases are not acceptable. I can go into detail about how they were formulated later. This was a categorical statement saying that, yes, this was the cause of death, ranging from that down to a very low probability.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Professor, can you enlighten the Chamber or all of us as to why it is that the Potocari autopsy reports are more cautious or reluctant or skeptical in reaching or indicating a cause of death versus the Sandici autopsy reports which do, based on the same descriptions that are in the autopsy reports, they do reach a cause of death, and they do reach a cause of injury. Can you explain why there is this apparent divergence in approach?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had occasion to analyse the two locations in parallel. The summary of my conclusions would be this: Potocari, the location of Potocari, was treated in 2006, meaning the seven bodies, six males and one female. The Sandici location was examined in 2004. I was trying to come to a certain conclusion as to why the conclusions from 2004 were written the same identical way they were for Potocari, whereas in one case we have cause of death and the other case we don't. It is my presumption, and I believe it to be realistic, that the same autopsy team in 2004 working at Sandici was under a degree of influence of people from international organisations who were of the opinion that the cause of death could be ascertained, as can be seen from my previous finding for the other -- for certain other locations. In the meantime, there was criticism by the professionals in the field, and I testified in the meantime; and that is why I presume that -- why the same autopsy experts were more cautious in the case of Potocari when drawing conclusions on the cause of death. The professional public that was closely following the research and the testimonies here had a degree of influence; and they, hence, became more cautious in Potocari in the chapter concerning cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You used an expression -- well, at least in the translation it came across as "the professional public." What are you referring to when you refer to the professional public, if that expression makes any sense to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: When I use that term, I mean colleagues, forensic pathologists working nowadays in the area of the former Yugoslavia. I was the last secretary of the Forensic Pathologist Association of Yugoslavia, which fell apart when this country did. We all know each other. There are many new colleagues, whereas some senior ones retired. However, we all come from the same educational background. When I say "professional public," I don't mean only the professionals from Yugoslavia but also from other domains. I receive information from my colleagues working in the United Kingdom, in the US, in Canada. We discuss things among ourselves, and people talk about that. They were wondering how can the cause of death of a fully skeletonized body be ascertained, claiming that the cause of death was a gunshot injury, precisely described in the report. Why am I saying this? I can repeat what I said last time: The cause of death has to do exclusively with the pathological changes or traumas ante-mortem. Once the vital functions cease, that means that the cause of death was the event which caused the functions to cease. John Clark also confirms that. It can be done with a fresh body, if I may use that term. If that is missing, if there is no soft tissue but only bones, then there is only a possibility or a probability that the gunshot injury, which is very well described, then with a certain lower degree of probability can be associated with the cause of death. That's it. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Aside from your own, I believe you said that you testified sometime in the interval between 2004 and 2006. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. Testified where?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought I understood you to say that you had testified here between 2004 and --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I testified in this same case previously, explaining the notion of cause of death. However, it had to do with different locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No, I understand that. But you've described to the Chamber that there was a shift - and if I can use the expression - in the climate of professional opinion, as you've described it, that there was criticism; and I'm just wondering if you can provide some further specificity as to where that criticism came from. Or was it just criticism between or amongst -- in discussions between colleagues? I am just asking for more specificity as to what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: What I said was that there was discussion among us forensic experts. We discussed those things at our meetings, not questioning the people working on those cases. People were merely talking about things not being done fully professional or not according to the rules of the profession. Such were conversations between the people in that field. I know colleagues in Zagreb, Sarajevo, Belgrade, Montenegro, et cetera. When we see each other privately, we also discuss our work, our profession and its components. It is, therefore, my presumption that it was for that reason that in 2006 the same people who worked on both locations were more cautious when drafting their conclusions. This is, however, only my presumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'd now like to look at a different finding in your report, and this is at page 132 in e-court in the English and page 69 of the B/C/S version, which I believe is page 70 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, here at the bottom of the page, you state: "It is impossible to establish the exact cause of death... to establish the time of death... the time of burial... or the injury mechanism." Now, I'd like to focus your attention on the second and third of those conclusions, the time of death and time of burial. Can you please describe what forensic observations positively indicated to you from these autopsy reports that these remains, that these sets of remains were not all buried at the same time or that they were not all deceased at the same time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The only thing I was able to notice and to assess forensically were the three cases from Potocari and two cases from Sandici. The three from Potocari in the description of the remains found -- state that these were mummified. As for the two Sandici cases, it is stated that they were saponified. That is what I had in mind in brief. Mummification and saponification are putrefaction changes which occur on skeletal remains or parts of the soft tissue post-mortem. Mummification is such a process in which the tissue becomes dry as in a mummy, hence the word. As for saponification as a process in which the soft tissue reminds of soap; that is the degree of putrefaction. It is soapy in terms of consistency. For a layperson, it means nothing; for us, it means the following: If a body is in a saponified state or if there is traces of saponification, it means that that body spent a certain period of time in a humid environment. If there is mummification, that proves that the body was supposed to warm and dry air. What does it have to do with this? Well, I've been saying that all along, that is that the time death and the time of burial cannot be ascertained precisely because in terms of doctrine, those changes were not described properly. For example, in Potocari there are seven bodies, and according to the reports there were three of those that were mummified. And in Sandici, out of the 17 there were two bodies that were saponified. That is evidence. And all the other bodies were skeletonized without any soft tissue whatsoever. This means that the two bodies that were saponified and the three in Potocari that were mummified were subsequently brought to those locations. They were probably exposed to humid or dry air and then subsequently buried. The other bodies simply became skeletonized after burying, whereas these cases exhibited different characteristics. The degree of putrefaction in terms of saponification and mummification as opposed to the other cases shows that the time of burial or death was different. However, that cannot be ascertained at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you notice any other observations in the autopsy reports that would support the suggestion that not all -- the bodies were not all buried at the same time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In addition to the fact that in the same locality, in Potocari and in Sandici, that exhumations took place at different time intervals, and that after certain identification procedures were put in place, we saw that some bodies were buried in the broader area -- or rather, they were listed as missing at different time-periods, either in 1995 or other years. And I found some cases dating back to 1993, that they were killed then and found later and exhumed later. That means that the very fact that there is a different degree of putrefaction and different times of exhumation go to show that the way in which they were buried was different. There were different times and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Professor, I was thinking of positive indications in the autopsy reports other than what you've mentioned about the saponification and the mummification of certain of the remains, and I'm thinking perhaps whether there were any observations under the category of clothing that might be relevant here.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: One of the elements which can support this claim about the different time interval of when the bodies were found, for example, is that both in Potocari and Sandici, on the bodily remains, on the skeletal remains, in actual fact, we also found winter clothing, which -- the clothing found was winter clothing. So if the event occurred in July, the event we're discussing, then we can raise the question of why the clothing would have been the type of clothing worn in winter. I just made the observation. Now, the second point that I'd like to make in respect of clothing, well, the clothing was just enumerated; a list of what was found was compiled, and there were no descriptions as to any defects on the clothing, for example, which would be consistent with, for example, damage done when a gunshot wound is administered. So no descriptions of the clothing were made, damages to the clothing caused by projectiles, by gunshot wounds; whereas in Sandici, the conclusion was that everybody was killed as a result of gunshot wounds, whereas we see no evidence of that on the clothing. I don't see it in the autopsies, either, except in the three cases of those three bones that I mentioned earlier on. But as an -- as indirect evidence, with respect to the time of death and time of burial, we can explain that in one way or another, for example, if you find winter clothing in summer time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In respect of the Sandici autopsy reports, and we recall that in many of those cases gunshot wounds are considered -- or listed as the cause of death, is there something that you would have expected to find in those autopsy reports that you didn't find that would have supported that cause of death? And perhaps I should direct you to the section "Traces" in the autopsy reports.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In all these autopsy reports from Sandici, for example, in the set forms for the autopsy reports, it says the following: Under chapter F, for example, samples -- accepted samples, and then it says "projectiles" and then colon, dash. So I don't understand this, and I wrote that. Does that mean that these were projectiles which were found and taken as samples, or should it have described where they were taken from and described? On the one hand, we have clothing which doesn't have any damages from projectiles; on the other hand, the autopsy findings on the bones, they are just three bones in actual fact - I would like to underline that - just three bones, for which we can state that they have injuries which could correspond to projectiles fired from firearms. And now the question arises as to what we mean by "projectiles," and projectiles is in the plural, which means more than one. Were they taken as samples or where they -- should they have been described, descriptions of them given, or is this just a form -- an observation? Does it mean -- does the dash mean that there were no projectiles, or does it mean that a description should follow; whereas, there are no description this these reports. And moreover, in Sandici, for example, during the process of exhumation, that is to say, when the exhumation is conducted -- just let me take a moment to find this, please. What was found was one casing, one bullet casing, and that was the sole evidence in that -- in one case, I think it was, that the cartridge of a projectile was found. That is to say that that is the casing -- was the casing of a bullet fired from a firearm. That would be my answer. So those traces, the traces which should go to prove or at least be described there in that part, were not. They were not described in the autopsy report. No descriptions exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Perhaps you can tell us what kind of a description you would have expected to find in light of the cause of death under the category of Traces.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, where it is claimed that the cause of death was a gunshot wound, which is something that it says for all the cases in Sandici, you would have to have the following: A precise description on the bones showing that it was a gunshot wound, damages to the clothing -- on the remains of the clothing, and that in the body and in the bones or next to the body in the ground, a projectile might have been found. Whereas there is none of that, and yet it is claimed that the cause of death was a gunshot wound. We have injuries to the bones that are described - in Sandici, that is - but those descriptions do not correspond to gunshot injuries, gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now, I'd like to move from material that is strictly forensic and ask you some questions about what you might, and I believe you do, refer to in your report as external information. And at pages 76 to 77 of the English version of your report and page 74 of the B/C/S version - we don't need to bring it up on e-court - you refer to certain individuals who are listed as having disappeared at dates that are incompatible with having been killed as victims in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is precisely the reason for which I've been insisting on the proper type of forensic findings and descriptions and the proper identification, and that is precisely the reason I did that, because looking at this list of missing persons it would follow that the persons went missing at different time-periods in the course of 1995 and some even in 1993. They were killed in 1993 and then put on the list of missing persons linked to the Srebrenica case, and from that, we have a great probability of manipulation with a number of persons. Now, for me as a forensic expert to be absolutely certain or at least to be able to say this person died earlier on, this person died later on, I would need the forensic findings, the autopsy findings with all the relevant data in them, which would indicate that being the case, and that is why we always insist upon the fact that for Potocari and Sandici, we don't have enough elements to be able to establish the time of death precisely enough. So what the descriptions that should be found in the autopsy findings were not done in the best forensic manner, which makes it impossible to have a precise forensic identification of the individuals, or rather, when the individual was killed, when they were buried, and when they were found. This -- all these factors must correspond to the autopsy findings. Now, what I said for Potocari and Sandici, that we had three cases of mummification, and in Sandici I believe two cases of saponification, goes to confirm the different time intervals at which the bodies were buried and found in that particular area.

utterances.text: Professor Dunjic, there is also external evidence, again, non-forensic evidence in this case that a certain number of individuals, perhaps as many as six, may have died or been killed while inside the DutchBat compound whose remains are unaccounted for. utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, six persons died on the premises of the base at Potocari in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In the autopsy reports, there are no elements based on which I can either confirm or deny that based on the description of the corpses I see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Sir, are there any other items or anomalies that you observed in the reports that you reviewed that you would like to tell the Chamber about?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, for both sites, Sandici and Potocari, a general conclusion drawn from these autopsy reports that were presented and that I analysed would be that there is a total lack of transparency and an impossibility of verifying the data. In the anthropological part, they state that the individual is male, the estimated age is stated, and the estimated height, to mention but these examples. But there is not a single numerical parameter that would enable me to check that, whether that was really a man aged 60, 1 metre 70 tall, and whether it was a man at all. That's what I call intransparency. Only ready-made conclusions were presented, conclusions that are stated in this report. So it's for you to believe or disbelieve. I as an expert do not believe until I can verify whether it's really true, and this applies to all of it. And it's not only about lack of transparency; it also applies to injuries, especially to injuries. In one case, an injury is described as a fracture, as a defect, as a general "concept," in inverted commas, of something that was seen. But in Potocari, the cause of death cannot be established. At Sandici, for the same finding the conclusion is gunshot as cause of death, which is nonsense. That's inconsistency between what was found and the conclusion drown from it.
